reviews.text: [i][b][h1]Noah的机车驱魔之旅[/h1][/b][/i] [h3]标签[/h3] 卡牌构筑类rogue、男主、驱魔、重复遭遇合理化叙事 [h3]简介[/h3] 前神父现驱魔人Noah来到了一座被地狱侵蚀的城市之中，追寻着名为Malys的恶魔 [h3]时长[/h3] EA初见一周目一个半小时左右，只有一幕，最终BOSSMalys并没有出现。 时间主要花在看英文上了，包含一些暂时离开的挂机时间，然后游戏内统计30分钟？ [h3]评价[/h3] +剧情 作为卡牌构筑类Rogue，该游戏走向了重复遭遇合理化的方向。如果你不理解的话，可以参考Hades，作为冥界王子将复活合理化，流程中遭遇的人物、敌人剧情连贯化，前阵子我还玩过一个Knock on the Coffin Lid，也是以从棺材中复活将游戏进行合理rogue化。 而这个游戏呢，目前我还没开第二局，仅在第一局内，就有三个人物会重复出现。剧情连贯，并合理解释为什么会重复出现（其中一个人大概是Noah的守护天使，到处跟踪你，在你走到巷子里时在前面堵你……）。再加上David的写作，短短几次遭遇几个人物的特点就很鲜明了，还顺带塑造主角（过往之类的），只缺一个中文…… EA只有英文，不知道正式版有没有计划添加其它语言？ +手绘 我还是挺喜欢这个画风的，但是有些地方感觉太EA了？不过我也对这些不太懂，对上感觉就行。 ▲卡牌构筑的独特性 对于玩过不少卡牌游戏的我，这个游戏特殊在于：burn（燃烧）。你可以随时将一牌燃烧转化为一费（某绿色杂技大师馋哭了，另外注意这个并没有消耗掉牌，而是进弃牌堆） 比较特殊，但是也带来了个问题就是，左脚踩右脚很容易无敌，我在这一局流程内抓了不少摸牌、两三张Salt Prison（1费给三张0费打3，也就是猎宝的刀舞）以及一些附带Miracle词条的牌（非摸牌阶段摸上来时0费）。所以熟悉的玩家已经知道怎么无敌了，不懂的我来解释下。 Salt Prison几乎=白拿两费，一张2费摸3的牌=不亏不赚，但是如果摸上来带miracle那就血赚，好牌多抓，摸牌抓上来摸牌，然后就一回合秒了BOSS。 所以数值可能是个问题？我需要多打几把验证下。 -UI 拿牌的界面周围黑边会把最后一张牌的提示遮掉，五张卡时缩得很小； 卡牌上的词条没有高亮； 鼠标在手牌那边拖动时并不准确，有时候一直在左右两张牌跳，死活选不到中间某一张牌。 -BUG 1.恶魔的意图有时候显示并不正确； 2.遇到一个叫做“Camped out”的事件，最后curio和牌二选一。curio显示“#curioname#“，选了闪退…… 3.修女（3费队友，烧卡时造成1点伤害），玩久后游戏卡顿非常明显，重启好了 -配音 事件并没有配音，纯文字。只有战斗时用牌的时候有些吟唱声。 不过42块钱我可能要求太多了？ [h3]结语[/h3] 比较EA，但是有潜力，背景设置很喜欢，我很怀念被砍掉的剧版《驱魔人》，看看游戏正式版怎么样

[h1]EA review:[/h1] * Visuals and overall atmosphere - superb and unique enough * Gameplay mechanics - fun but underexplored so far * Gameplay content - only 1 act, several simple card archetypes * Writing - decent but too damn long, having 4 pages of non-voiced flavor text before each fight is too much Overall state - promising but very early access, I've seen almost all there is in a little more than 1hr, played some more to be sure -------------------------------------------------- [h1]Full release upd.: [/h1] game has barely changed * Visuals: excellent * Writing: excessive * Gameplay: extremely underexplored, surface level deckbuilding with barely any archetypes and synergies, just go for bigger damage number and you're golden * Difficulty settings: they literally didn't think about it and slapped it on top, highest difficulty makes enemies deal half your hp in 1 attack while having so much hp it would take at least 5-8 turns to finish only ONE OF SEVERAL COMBAT PHASES Conclusion: never let artists make games just by themselves (I'm an artist, I would know). I wish I could refund but that's the risk of supporting EA games I guess. I guess I've played myself, expecting gameplay depth from a dev known for a visual novel game.

I wanted to like this game. I want to support indie studios. I love deck builders. The art style is fantastic, even if im not a religiously knowledgeable person and seeing this Constantine-inspired deckbuilder, the thematic trappings are still quite neat. This game as a game just isn't good. The UI is clunky, cards are poorly explained in tooltips, there is no collection function to examine cards outside of during a run when they're in your deck. You cannot see the entire pool of cards, upgrades, or relics. The cards have no indicted rarity or exclusivity apparently based on your starting poke- 1 of 3 relics. The deck archetypes do seem to function differently. One seems to build around a combo deck with an ally and playing lots of cards for damage. One imitates the Barricade/Body Slam combo from Ironclad in StS, and the third seems to just rely on face tanking a lot of damage because you can get to a point of essentially infinite healing and then timing that deck to explode your healing stacks as a single nuke. In general though, the gameplay is incredibly slow. There is a sweet spot for deck size, somewhere between 10-15 cards depending on if you have cards with card draw, or ones that are removed from the deck during an encounter after being played. And then... run your engine? There are essentially 3 different engines as i pointed out... but after playing with all 3, beating the final boss a few times to get an achievement for the TRUE ENDING (but there is an achievement for something that clearly happens after), I am just left feeling, the gameplay is incredibly clunky, samey, the enemies never test your deck in different ways, and your success will vary wildly depending on if you get some key relics or additional cards. The game uses a StS style map of encounters, where you choose a path. Very few of the encounters are other than fights. You have 3 different stores, and card upgrades, and relics are expensive. The card rewards are wildly random, as i don't have a collection i can't say what i haven't seen, but a huge number of cards are literally useless. You do not want to be adding lots of cards to your deck. So getting 6 cards that do different attack styles isn't worth it. You'd rather have a small deck, and redraw the same cards. It is hard to loop your deck with the candle mechanic, and going infinite is impossible as far as i know, but you don't need it. The build to just cheese and armor up until you have enough to cast your bomb attack that deals 1 damage per armor you have a few times in succession, will win every time, because you're never going to lose health, and you will scale faster than the enemy every time. I don't think the difficulty is what's wrong. Sure 1 build I found to be winnable 100% of the time, but the mechanics themselves are just clunky. As i said earlier, since the enemies aren't very reactive, its just that this build cheeses the enemy. They simply cannot react. Finally, I will say, i skipped the story. Basically all of it. So I can't comment to the quality of the writing. I just wanted to see what this deckbuilder offers. The most interesting thing is the mechanic of using any card as an energy to play another. And so it does feel like there should be meaningful choices in what you burn for energy and what you can play. But ultimately there isn't. I do like that what you've burned cant be re burned in the same round, so you cannot go infinite. But that doesn't mean you can't cheese. Its just you have to find the rhythm. But it isn't hard to find that rhythm, and once you do, you're just clicking buttons until you win. It is boring. If the developers wanted to at least make the UX better, having a COLLECTION tab would good. I really just cannot forgive any deckbuilder-type game releasing into 1.0 more than 10 years after Slay the Spire set a standard, and not at least doing what any player of the genre should know is important. The fact I do not know what all the cards are, or relics, or if its all 1 giant pool, or whats exclusive to your starting deck or not, is kinda ridiculous. Further, many times where i got to a store to buy new cards, I would frequently see the same card in 2 of the 3 slots. I assume its a bug, but it happened every single run i've had at least once. Not knowing what the upgrades for a card are until you're in the store that lets you upgrade and only seeing the upgrades for your deck? Its a huge factor in whether I take a card offered after a fight, but not knowing how it upgrades? That isn't a good design decision. Especially because this is StS-like upgrades; that is, there is only a single upgrade, not like Monster train where the upgrades are customisable, or a bunch of others, where there might be 2 or even 3 upgrade options. Finally, all the enemies feel the same. They have a flow. Set up, block, and attack. It sounds the same as in StS or Monster Train or any number of other deckbuilders, but in this one, there are very few alternative forms of pressure. Its super basic. I hate to say it, but i regret spending my money on this 6 hours in and unable to get a refund. This game just isn't worth it. Even if you think you like the aesthetic.

This review was quite difficult to write because I really care for Summerfall Studios and wish them all the best. I also saw the difficult path Malys had to take to get to release. I was one of those "wannabe Kickstarter backers", even though I wasn't really interested in a "roguelike deckbuilder" to be honest - I just wanted to support the studio that gave me so many great moments with Stray Gods, their previous project, and I believed in their ability to create a good game. Unfortunately, as of right now, Malys feels more like *parts* of a good game to me. I'll give Summerfall credit where credit is due: it seems like they had to make some tough decisions about what to focus on during such a short development period and they made the right choice by focusing on the core gameplay (and especially the deck-building aspect) - it's definitely viable, feels good and could form the basis of a good game. I also really like the art style, and I think the semi-black and white aesthetic suits the game and I assume allowed the developer to save resources a bit. For me, the Malys started to fail after about 2-2,5 hours, after I've already done a few runs. The game is quite difficult, and simple luck plays too big a role in your run's success. Sure, the game has difficulty settings and a few modes that make things easier, but here's the thing – I *want* a challenge, and as a player, I don't *really* want to give up. I'd like difficulty reduction to be *earned*, either through my personal gameplay experience (i.e. "now I know better") or through some kind of meta-progression. Unfortunately, the game isn't deep enough at the moment for the first thing to work properly (it doesn't feel like I've got a lot to improve in my strategy), and the second - is nonexistent. My next major complaint is about narrative design. The text vignettes that precede each encounter become old pretty fast. They simply don't fit into a game that relies on repetition and have a negative impact on the pacing. I usually don't like to skip anything in games, but I started doing it here - but even then I had problems because the dialogue skipping UX in Malys is also a bit flawed. So it unfortunately became quite boring pretty fast. I felt like it's too much of a grind to move on and I wasn't too invested to do that - even with the possible difficulty reduction. Once again, I sincerely wish Summerfall all the best and remain interested in their future projects should they come up with any. And I feel kinda bad writing this negative review. But at the same time, I firmly believe in honest criticism, even if it may hurt a little.

So, the concept and visuals are really strong here and that's what drew me to this game originally. Unfortunately after a single extended play session, I gave up on the story, as it lacks the interest of making choices. ultimately all the story scenarios kind of blend into one thing more or less, and at the end of the story blurb you inevitably fight the demon possessing someone. No exceptions, no choices that impact the fight, no evading the fight, just encounter possessed person, try and excise the demon. rinse & repeat. So I started skipping story stuff after about 90 min of this type of thing. Very disappointing for someone who loves story in their games. Unfortunately the combat design & difficulty felt really uneven, Lesser Demons came across as incredibly easy while many of the greater demons & bosses felt almost unbeatable. It seems like there is no strategy that can help you at a certain point. These greater demons just apply infinite stacks of damage increasing debuffs you cannot avoid, and then kill you when you get a bad draw or when the damage becomes too much, even if you ward the damage of the attack the increased damage stack still applies, and many of these encounters turn into real drags of both sides continually mitigating damage, each having 100ish hit points. oh and the greater demons have 3 distinct phases, making for a Long, monotonous encounter. There's something interesting about the core system for playing vs burning cards and selecting who to target, but the actual card mechanics were pretty uninspired for the most part. I have yet to see any truly interesting combos that you can pull off with clever maneuvering or by prepping a lot of actions for the following turns. Also there does not seem to be any Rougelike meta progression. so the uneven & punishing difficulty sets you back to square 1 if you lose, and the random "story events" do little to keep it fresh. since they don't differ much and offer zero choice.

After finishing the game, getting the true ending and all the achivements, I feel qualified to give my review. First of all the Good: The combat is SO much fun! I've never played any serious deckbuilders like this before but I absolutely love the comat in this game. Burning cards in order to play other cards is such a unique mechanic that really makes you think about what you're doing and keeps you on your toes at all times. I also really enjoy some of the different synergies for certain cards. The art is incredible as well, the thick lineart and the black and white coloring gives the world such a depressing feel to it which works perfectly for the game. The way each character design looks unique and different from each other really makes me feel connected to these characters. The music and sound design is really immersive too. The way each exorcism has the sounds of the possessed screaming in pain does such a good at showing the horror of what's happening. And by far the best part of the game is the story. I mean, this was obvious coming from the studio that made Stray Gods, but I was still surprised by how much I was engrossed in the story. The way that the narrative made each death feel impactful was so cool and rivals Hades for the way it weaves narrative into the rougelike/lite style. The characters are so well written and I love learning about the past and conflicts of your allies. Now the Bad: While it's really interesting to have each encounter open with a storylet to explain what's happening, it can get tedious when you see the same storylet three times in the same run. I think there should have been a larger variety of these storylets to prevent so much repetition. The same thing goes for the NPC art. It's really well drawn and I love the designs, but it gets a little boring seeing the same character 7 times in one run. Overall, Malys is an incredibly fun game with a great narrative. Both of my issues stem from an (unfortunately) smaller budget than they wanted. I was one of the backers of the kickstarter and I really wished it succeded so that Sumerfall would've had the budget to make this game even better. However, this game is still so much fun and I encourage anyone on the fence to check it out.

I hope the Game keeps being Mantained, this is a real Hidden Gem that deserves to get some more further Development and Attention. Also, there's a very Annoying Bug regarding the Card "Reversal of Fortune": it's supposed to put the Last Card Played or Discarded on the TOP of the Draw Pile, but it Most certainly DOES NOT do that! It's a shame, since the Combo with the Miracle Cards being put on the Top and then being Drawed is very useful, but it doesn't actually do that, most of the times, because it doesn't do what the Card says it does; it just shuffles the Card in the Draw Pile. There's also a Similar issue with the Pocket Keyword: if "Read the Signs" Discards a Card with Pocket – might be worth poiting out that the Pocket in Question was given by the "Prepare" Card – not only the Card doesn't get Drawn as it should, since it should put the Discarded Card on the Top of the Draw Pile, but it doesn't even get Put into the Draw Pile AT ALL; which is contratticting to the text on the Cards.

I cannot recommend this game, although I wanted to like it due to the theme and atmosphere. Here's why: Major: 1) The game has too many options for what can be done with a deck making it difficult to get good synergy with mechanics. It feels like the project started overly ambitious and too much was added that never got trimmed down with balancing. 2) In spite of point 1 the game is very easy to win once you understand a few things, the primary being that since cards are the energy source anything, that draws cards is often paying for itself coupled with miracle cards that are free when you draw them after your turn begins. 3) Even knowing how to win every fight with no real risk the fights are very long meaning its boring due to the lack of pressure and also because it takes so long to end. 4) Despite the fights being so long the game is very short. I beat it twice in my 15 hours of playtime. There is a hidden Steam achievement still so there probably is another story bit to uncover but I'd rather not. 5) The game crashed 3 or 4 times during my playtime for seemingly no reason which is pretty annoying after investing so many rounds into a boring fight then being forced to do it all over again. Nit-picky: 1) The story snippets before each fight are cool at first but being presented with 2 pages of text you have already ready for the fifth time feels bad. The story itself was mediocre in my opinion with the plot twists feeling cookie cutter. 2) The UI is bad. It is very frequently the case that clicking on a reward directly on the box multiple times does not register the selection which is sloppy programming. Also when being presented with card rewards their upgrades should be viewable since they often dramatically change how valuable a card is.

First, the positives: the game is dripping with style, and a lot of the demon designs are sick. The writing is solid, though not enough to stop me from getting frustrated with the sheer amount of it after a while. I enjoyed the concept of the central gameplay mechanic— "burning" (discarding) your cards in exchange for mana to spend further cards— but I felt like the deckbuilding options available didn't capitalise on it in a way that is satisfying to me. The game employs a branching map, but I never felt like my decisions were in anyway meaningful (or enjoyable). The deckbuilding too rigid and the passive relics I found too weak to ever make me get that dopamine rush of going infinite, or feeling triumphantly powerful over these unholy enemies. It felt sloggy, even when I was winning. Where the game really grinds to halt is the Greater Demon fights, which for some reason have three phases and gigantic health pools, but are only worth a paltry 40 currency (normal fights grant 18, and are an order of magnitude easier). Narratively I like the concept of having to discover a demon's true name before you can really begin to lay into it, I just wish there was a mechanic rewarding meta-knowledge to shortcut the process. All-in-all I was disappointed, I wanted to like this thing but it never really clicked for me.

I'm kind of mixed about this one. I was interested because I do like roguelites, and the involvement of David Gaider and Liam Essler was of course a huge plus. Coming to Malys from Slay the Spire and similar, I felt myself noticing some balance weirdness - the glow/light deck feels so much stronger that I barely even tried the other two. A reliable source of regen, barring the few demons that can snuff your candles? Yes please. There's a reason that many roguelites severely limit availability of healing. Okay, so maybe it's not going to convert anyone who's already married to Slay the Spire, but Malys oozes style. From the gorgeous opening track to its magnificent boss themes, the music really shines. With some roguelites, I mute the soundtrack and listen to a podcast instead, but that felt weirdly heretical here. The limited voice acting (provided by Summerfall staff) is evocative and left me wanting more, with the exception of Noah's slightly too-frequent combat lines, since you do hear them quite a lot. And the character designs! Oh my goodness. The angel was far and away my favorite, for reasons I cannot touch on without enormous spoilers, but Lydia and Gideon really shone as well. Something as simple as turning merchants into characters who have a major role in your story added so much for me. I also very much appreciated Malys for its narrative and thematic dimension. The flashes of text prior to exorcisms hint at what you'll face, and enemy types repeat but on the whole are mechanically quite varied. Greater demons include creative abilities that reward the player's flexibility, and their designs are spectacular, as magnificent as they are grotesque. I guess my biggest complaint is that, depending on deck, some of the greater exorcisms especially can be really, really drawn out. This is more merciful than some games might be, in that rolling in with a so-so deck doesn't result in you heading back to the start, but it can unfortunately pall. So, tldr, this is one you play if you're the kind of freak who plays roguelites for the story and you don't mind it being effectively a one and done, rather than an endless game with a drip-feed of content. I appreciate that this is a game you can experience in full in a pretty reasonable amount of time while still being a fun one to pick up and put down. Do I recommend this game? I think so, but with reservations. It isn't going to compete with the big names in the genre, but that's fine, it isn't trying to. It's a gorgeously atmospheric and tightly-written story about the world's most dejected priest and his situationship with a nonbinary angel. If that appeals, you're probably the target audience.

Malys is easy to learn while still having enough depth to allow for a lot of flexibility with how you construct your deck. The narrative elements are solid, I think the game does a good job of varying the descriptions and dialogue between each run even though some of the standard encounter descriptions can get repetitive after several runs. I'm really enjoying my time with this so far.

Genuinely fun enough game, similar to slay the spire but with less memorisation of enemy attack patterns and a more reasonable difficulty ramping. Could use a rebalancing of some decks archetypes, the most interesting deck is allies but is also the weakest of the decks. Card draw with miracles, and defensive heavy decks seem the strongest. As a suggestion I would say the ability to reroll shops would be worth while, in particular the card and curios shops would allow the player to be more flexible in their deck building. The unique shop types are probably the most interesting part of the game.

Game is wildly unbalanced. Your entire run will be hard locked if you run into Timult as the greater demon RNG. He has an ability called Pact, which he places on himself and you. All healing or damage directly dealt is shared. One of the starting items is the ability to generate glow which heals you at end of turn. If you deal enough damage to expel him, click expel, the end of turn effect will give him half your heal and break the expel. There is no way around this. Unplayable until resolved. And considering there haven't been any patches in 2026 I assume the game is abandonware. Multi-hour run ruined because of bad mechanics.

A pretty fun card game with some interesting decks. Biggest complaint is you get so much repeat dialogue that when you get new dialogue you only realize it's new after the second or third slide. I wish there was a way to look back. Overall pretty good.
It's a cool idea, nice mechanics, but the game doesn't have much replayability.

I actually found this game to be extremely compelling, and intensely disappointing. First, the narrative elements are mostly well done, and add an extra layer to the game which is captivating. I stopped to read basically every unique encounter because they were all so well written, from each of the characters who act as merchants basically, to the simple descriptions leading up to even basic enemy encounters, which are worth reading through. The overall atmosphere that is cultivated and especially, ESPECIALLY, the visual design is probably some of the best that I have ever come across in a game, ever. Some of the enemy designs are breathtaking. I would like to think that generally I have a really high tolerance for horror media, I engage with horror media a lot, but some of the enemy designs here are actually, legitimately unsettling. Especially the mini-boss ones which are illustrated to be staring literally directly at you, it's actually slightly hard to pull your eyes off of them to look down at the cards, it's a borderline immersive experience. The gameplay mechanics, when they work and everything goes well, are super fun. I like the resource mechanics more than something like Slay the Spire, especially because of how all of the mechanics are carefully and intricately weaved into the aesthetics of the game's setting. Unfortunately, I give this game a thumbs up because I want to support it somehow, even though a positive Steam review means basically nothing at this point, but I can't seriously say that I recommend it broadly. But there is so much potential here it's crazy. This could be such, such an incredible game. But it looks totally and completely abandoned. Like the production value is so clearly insane. A complex, obviously professionally very well written narrative with tons of dialogue, so many incredibly detailed illustrations, it's obvious that a team of people really worked on this. But there's like not even more than a couple hundred Steam reviews and a tiny amount of social media presence which fizzled out like a year ago. Just, how is that even possible!? Regardless, it looks like the last update was over 6 months ago, and going off of how much attention this is getting I can't even blame them for abandoning it. It must be kind of crushing to make something this good and to have it not be appreciated in the way that it should. But gosh, so much of the experience of playing it just sucks. It's buggy beyond belief. Mechanics not working like they should. Visual glitches. Dialogue glitching and just not playing. Random blank screens. It's non-stop. And the balancing is horrible. The glow deck is totally broken, you just snowball every single fight and it's clear that an appropriate counter to the glow mechanic was never implemented. But the initial damage based deck is horrible. You get whittled down as debuffs get stacked harder and harder while the deck lacks both resources and defense. And like other people have pointed out, the length of the mini-boss fights is ridiculous. I had one which went over 40 turns, they can literally take like 30 minutes if you really draw it out and truly fight for your win. It sucks to play the game knowing that none of these things will ever be fixed, and this wonderful example of how good a video game can be as an interactive art-form will just rot further into obscurity. Most gamers would probably be immediately hostile to these sorts of things but it's nice that Malys includes elements of diversity. It's done in a way which I didn't find to be patronizing, othering, and without drawing unnecessary attention to theses topics. UPDATED THOUGHTS: After playing another 20 or so hours I've found that Malys has undeniably grown on me. Once you get a hang of the flow of each "exorcism" then the balancing feels much more even across each deck and run. At first I thought that the miniboss-esque exorcisms were too long, with three phases and several hundred health usually for each phase 2 and 3, I've found now that it's really not bad at all and once you have a decent deck going you'll just completely blow through everything without any resistance. At first I thought that the game was stacked against the player, but now I'm consistently having runs where it feels basically impossible to die, when you have like 7 phantom, 200 shield, and a mini-boss at like 20 shackle consistently. Card draw is really the number 1 thing, you can get like three or four hands in a single turn while also cutting the cost of pretty much all cards down to 0 for a whole turn. Actually feels really good to pull off. Still, it's just obviously an abandoned, discarded gem of a game. Love the characters too, they're all interesting in their own right and feel well fleshed out. It's nice to see how the MC's and other character's relationships grow, I really like the MC and the hot demon guy as a pair, if this game had the audience it deserved there would be literally so much fanfic stuff of those them.
